doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: The studio scene and recreating 'I Can't Get Started'
summary: Network staff bands disappeared; on a recreation date for Enoch Light he played Berigan's solo note for note.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: So the studio scene became pretty healthy in those years in New York.

Yeah. Well there were three networks with the major, even symphony orchestra and a commercial band of 25 or so on staff. And then that all died. Why? I don’t really know. It’s like the business in the Catskill Mountains. It used to be a thriving, thriving thing and then it died. I can’t really understand.
When you got a call to do a recording or a studio date, did you necessarily know who it was going to be for, or what the music was going to be like?

No. I know there was an exception to that that I used to do — Enoch Light had a record — he had two or three different record companies you know. And he was doing these recreations of band hits so called. And they wanted to do “I Can’t Get Started.” And the date was on a Monday morning at 10 A.M. and I hadn’t played over the weekend or anything, and they did call me, the record company, and said Dick has written, he wrote out all the notes, I don’t need them I knew them. But they said he wants you to play “I Can’t Get Started.” That was not the one that’s on this record, it was like an actual re- creation of the original, he wrote the chart exactly note for note. And I played the solo note for note. But they said — this is ten o’clock — we don’t want you to come in without chops, we want to let you know what you’re up against. But most of the time you didn’t know. You’d go in, sit down, they’d hand out some charts.
